title: Wage growth holds at 3.7%, real pay is finally ahead of the cost of living again
excerpt: Pay rises across Australia ran at 3.7 per cent over the year to June. With the cost of living at 2.7 per cent, that means real pay is now growing for the fourth quarter in a row.
body:
Pay rises across Australia ran at 3.7 per cent over the year to June, the same as the March number, according to the Wage Price Index from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (the government agency that collects economic data). The result was a touch softer than the 3.8 per cent economists had forecast.

Public-sector workers, including teachers, nurses, and public servants, got the biggest pay rises at 4.1 per cent, driven by ongoing union agreements. Private-sector workers, people in retail, hospitality, construction, and most office jobs, got 3.6 per cent, the slowest since late 2022.

The more important number is what it means in real terms. The cost of living (called CPI, or Consumer Price Index) was running at 2.7 per cent over the same period. That means your pay rise is 1.0 per cent more than the cost of living, so your real spending power went up by about 1 per cent over the year. For someone on $85,000 a year, that is roughly an extra $850 of real spending power, not a lot, but the fourth consecutive quarter of positive real-wage growth.

Our take: this is the strongest real pay growth in four years. The 'cost of living crisis' argument is finally over, pay is now keeping up with prices. If you are up for a pay review or a job interview, this is the data to bring to the table. White-collar workers in tech and finance are typically getting more than 3.7 per cent, while retail and hospitality are closer to 3.5 per cent.
whatItMeans: If you are up for a pay review: Use 3.7 per cent as your starting number. Anything under 3 per cent in 2026 is effectively a pay cut once you account for the cost of living.

If you work in the public sector: Your union agreements are delivering the strongest pay growth. If you are a teacher, nurse, or public servant mid-agreement, you are getting above-cost-of-living pay rises built in.

If you are a hiring manager: Labour costs are still going up faster than they did before COVID. Budget 4 per cent pay growth into your 2026 forecasts. Anything below that is a real-terms pay cut for your staff.

If you are watching the Reserve Bank: A 3.7 per cent pay growth print is consistent with the Reserve Bank's view that the jobs market is still tight enough to keep inflation sticky. That makes an early interest rate cut less likely.
